items.source_reference_title_replacement: Allen Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, section 1.3 (covering and homotopy lifting), Proposition A.4 (CW complexes are locally contractible, printed p. 522), and section 3.H (the lifted cellular structure and deck-group-ring chains, printed p. 335)

edits.replacement: [F1] By [[lem-the-complement-of-an-oriented-link-is-a-connected-smooth-three-manifold]], $X_L$ has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex: choose a finite CW complex $Z$ and homotopy inverses $h:X_L\to Z$, $g:Z\to X_L$, with $gh\simeq\mathrm{id}_{X_L}$ and $hg\simeq\mathrm{id}_Z$. The path-connected $X_L$ makes $Z$ path-connected: every $z$ is joined to $h(g(z))$ by the latter homotopy, and images under $h$ of paths in $X_L$ join these image points. As the quoted local input of Hatcher, Proposition A.4, every CW complex has arbitrarily small contractible open neighbourhoods; hence $Z$ is locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected. No based homotopy or retraction is assumed ([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]).

edits.target: Facts & Assumptions, [F3], append path lifting source to covering facts
edits.replacement: [F3] A subgroup of the fundamental group of a suitable base classifies a connected covering, and a based map lifts exactly when its induced subgroup lies in the covering subgroup. A normal covering subgroup gives a regular cover, whose deck group is the fundamental-group quotient and acts transitively on each fibre ([[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]]). Paths have unique lifts, homotopies lift from an initial lift, and connected-domain lifts agreeing at one point are equal ([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]], [[thm-covering-space-lifting-criterion]], [[thm-path-lifting-for-covering-maps]], [[thm-homotopy-lifting-for-covering-maps]], [[thm-uniqueness-of-lifts-from-a-connected-space]], [[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]). Singular homology is functorial and homotopic maps induce equal maps ([[prop-singular-chains-and-homology-are-covariantly-functorial]], [[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]]); homotopy equivalences induce isomorphisms ([[thm-homotopy-equivalences-induce-isomorphisms-on-singular-homology]]).

1.1 *Transporting the cover.* Set $z_0=h(x_0)$ and transport the total-linking homomorphism to $\varphi_Z=\varphi\circ h_*^{-1}$ on $\pi_1(Z,z_0)$. Here $h_*$ is an isomorphism: a homotopy inverse gives its inverse after transport of basepoints along the homotopies; a moving-basepoint homotopy conjugates loop classes by its basepoint path. Such conjugation does not change the homomorphism to the abelian group $\mathbb Z$. Classify the connected regular cover $\widetilde Z\to Z$ by $\ker\varphi_Z=h_*K$, and name the deck generator corresponding to $1\in\mathbb Z$ by $t$. The lifting criterion supplies $\widetilde h:\widetilde X_L\to\widetilde Z$; choose its value at a point over $x_0$. If a loop at $x_0$ has total linking $1$, its lift joins that point to its $t$-translate; its image under $h$ also has value $1$ under $\varphi_Z$. Path-lift uniqueness gives $\widetilde h(t\widetilde x_0)=t\widetilde h(\widetilde x_0)$. The maps $\widetilde h\,t$ and $t\,\widetilde h$ lift the same base map and have connected domain, so uniqueness makes them equal everywhere. Thus $\widetilde h$ is equivariant. [A1, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 *The lifted homology isomorphism.* Transport basepoints along a path from $g(z_0)$ to $x_0$. Since $g$ is a homotopy inverse, its induced isomorphism carries $\ker\varphi_Z$ onto $K$; the basepoint-path conjugations are harmless for these normal kernels. The lifting criterion therefore supplies a lift $\widetilde g:\widetilde Z\to\widetilde X_L$. Lift the homotopies $gh\simeq\mathrm{id}_{X_L}$ and $hg\simeq\mathrm{id}_Z$ from $\widetilde g\widetilde h$ and $\widetilde h\widetilde g$ respectively. Each endpoint lifts the identity of its base. In a connected regular cover it equals a deck transformation: choose the unique deck transformation with the same image at one point and apply lift uniqueness. Thus on singular homology both composites are automorphisms, being induced by deck homeomorphisms. Consequently $\widetilde h_*$ is injective and surjective; its equivariance from step 1.1 makes it a $\Lambda$-linear isomorphism. In particular $A_L\cong H_1(\widetilde Z;\mathbb Z)$ as $\Lambda$-modules. No lifted homotopy endpoint was required to be the identity. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

2.1 *Finite generation and presentation.* Give $\widetilde Z$ the lifted CW structure of the standard covering-cell construction (Hatcher, section 3.H, printed p. 335): lift the characteristic disks of $Z$, with their orientations; the lifted open cells are precisely the components over the base open cells. The deck group freely and transitively permutes the lifts of each base cell. Choosing one lift and orientation for each of the finitely many base cells therefore gives a bounded cellular chain complex $C_*$ of finite free $\Lambda$-modules, with deck-linear differentials. Cellular comparison identifies $A_L$ with $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_2$. By [F4], the kernel in the finite free module $C_1$ is finitely generated, and so is its quotient $A_L$. The kernel of a finite free surjection onto $A_L$ is again finitely generated by [F4], giving a finite presentation. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.2]

edits.operation: Replace the text 'by [F6] and step 1.1' with 'by [F1] and [F6]'; the remaining specialization/Euler/torsion steps can remain unchanged.

proof_audit: Unbased homotopy inverse suffices. Homology composites are automorphisms because lifted homotopy endpoints are deck transformations; this yields bijectivity without asserting normalized lifted endpoints or equivariant inverse homotopies.

The finite CW is path connected and has covering classification hypotheses by explicit Hatcher A.4 input. Kernel transport respects basepoint changes because the total-linking map has abelian codomain.
Only h needs explicit equivariance: once h_* is a bijective Lambda-linear map, its inverse is automatically Lambda-linear.

Finite cellular chains alone do NOT imply finitely generated homology over an arbitrary ring. Here the explicit Noetherian submodule supplier furnishes the essential kernel finiteness, then another kernel application furnishes finite presentation.

The retained knot torsion argument uses a bounded finite complex, generic differential rank at least specialization rank, vanishing generic H_i for i≥2, H_0=Lambda/(t−1), and Euler characteristic 0. All remain valid for arbitrary finite CW homotopy model.
items.uncertainty: No mathematical obstruction identified to this route. Root should keep the lifted-CW construction concise and source-backed; it is standard cover cellular structure, not a finite triangulation or compact-exterior claim. No independent validation claim is made.

items.finding: Confirmed false matrix equality under the exact Artin supplier: F_sigma1sigma2=F_sigma1∘F_sigma2, so equal-label row Fox Jacobian multiplies C2 C1, while the defined coloured/Burau product is C1 C2. In n=3, C1=[[-t,1],[0,1]], C2=[[1,0],[t,-t]], J=[[-t,1],[-t^2,0]], B=[[0,-t],[t,-t]]. These matrices have the same characteristic determinant but are unequal.

dependency_changes.reason: The local Gram proof uses determinant multiplicativity, transpose invariance, and the Laurent integral domain. It does not require a fraction-field similarity or invertibility of G over the Laurent ring.

edits.target: Facts [F1], sentence 'Thus it is Morton's convention.'
edits.replacement: Thus the elementary meridian substitutions agree with Morton's displayed substitutions. This generator-level bridge does not identify the row Fox Jacobian of a composite with the matrix product ordered as the braid word.

[F2] **Literature input (the multivariable formula).** Morton's Theorem 1 (printed p. 3, with the complete proof on pp. 4–6) states $\Delta_{\widehat\beta\cup A}\doteq\det(I-x\,\overline B_\beta(t_1,\ldots,t_n))$ after $t_{\pi(j)}=t_j$. His matrix is exactly the product in [[def-coloured-reduced-burau-matrix]]: bottom string labels, labels of successive undercrossings read from the top, row entries $(a,-a,1)$, and product in the word order. This theorem is used here as a literature input. The local calculation below checks the equal-label Fox determinant under the library's ordinary function-composition convention; it does not assert a multivariable composite-Jacobian matrix equality.

[F8] Determinants are multiplicative and invariant under transpose over a commutative ring ([[thm-determinant-multiplicative]], [[thm-determinant-of-transpose]]). The Laurent ring $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ is an integral domain ([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]]); adjoining an independent Laurent variable preserves this property, since the extreme nonzero coefficient in a product cannot cancel.

1.2 **The equal-label Jacobian and its order.** Work over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ and send every ordinary meridian to $t$; all Artin automorphisms preserve this evaluation. Write $C_i=\overline C_i(t)$ and $\beta=\sigma_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_l}^{\varepsilon_l}$. In the partial-product basis, step 1.1 gives $F_{\sigma_i}(g_i)=g_{i+1}g_i^{-1}g_{i-1}$, so its evaluated row derivatives in columns $i-1,i,i+1$ are $t,-t,1$, truncated at the boundary. Its last row is $(0,\ldots,0,1)$. The inverse elementary map has inverse evaluated Jacobian, by differentiating the identity composite. For ordinary function composition the row Fox chain rule reads $D(F\circ H)=F(DH)\,DF$; after the invariant equal-label evaluation it reads $J_{F\circ H}=J_HJ_F$. Thus the full evaluated Jacobian has the form $\widetilde J_\beta=\begin{pmatrix}J_\beta&v\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ with $J_\beta=C_{i_l}^{\varepsilon_l}\cdots C_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}$, while $B_\beta=C_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots C_{i_l}^{\varepsilon_l}$ by [F4]. Differentiating the conjugation terms of the presentation in step 1.1 and deleting the axis column gives $\widetilde J_\beta-x^{-1}I_n$, hence determinant $(1-x^{-1})\det(J_\beta-x^{-1}I_{n-1})$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

1.3 **A common symmetric matrix.** Put $m=n-1$ and define the symmetric tridiagonal matrix $G$ over $\Lambda$ by $G_{ii}=(t+1)t^{m-i}$, $G_{i,i+1}=G_{i+1,i}=-t^{m-i}$, with all other entries zero. If $e_i$ is the $i$-th coordinate column and $\ell_i$ is the row with entries $t,-(t+1),1$ in columns $i-1,i,i+1$, again truncated, then $C_i=I+e_i\ell_i$ and $Ge_i=-t^{m-i}\ell_i^T$. Symmetry gives $e_i^TG=-t^{m-i}\ell_i$, so $C_i^TG=G-t^{m-i}\ell_i^T\ell_i=GC_i$. Multiplying by the inverse on both sides also gives $(C_i^{-1})^TG=GC_i^{-1}$. At $t=1$, $G$ is the tridiagonal matrix with diagonal $2$ and adjacent entries $-1$. Its determinants satisfy $d_0=1$, $d_1=2$, $d_m=2d_{m-1}-d_{m-2}$ by expansion in the last row, hence $d_m=m+1=n$. Thus $\det G$ is a nonzero Laurent polynomial. [F4, F8, step 1.2, algebra]

1.4 **The characteristic determinants agree.** The elementary identities of step 1.3 and the reverse order in step 1.2 give $B_\beta^TG=GJ_\beta$. Consequently $(I-xB_\beta^T)G=G(I-xJ_\beta)$. Taking determinants over the integral domain $\Lambda[x^{\pm1}]$, using [F8], and cancelling the nonzero factor $\det G$ yields $\det(I-xB_\beta)=\det(I-xJ_\beta)$. This proves the required determinant identity without asserting $J_\beta=B_\beta$ or that $G$ is invertible over $\Lambda$. [F8, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

2.1 **The axis formula.** For all component labels, the source theorem [F2] applies to exactly the labelled product and variable identifications of [F4], proving (1). Independently, in the equal-label calculation the deleted axis generator has $\varphi(x)=x\ne1$, so [F3] and step 1.2 give $\Delta_{\widehat\beta\cup A}(t,x)\doteq (1-x^{-1})\det(J_\beta-x^{-1}I_m)/(1-x)\doteq\det(I-xJ_\beta)$. Indeed $(1-x^{-1})/(1-x)=-x^{-1}$ and $\det(J_\beta-x^{-1}I_m)=(-x^{-1})^m\det(I-xJ_\beta)$, whose prefactors are Laurent units. Step 1.4 converts this into $\det(I-xB_\beta)$ in the library's composition convention. The multivariable assertion is the quoted theorem, while this local determinant calculation establishes the equal-label convention bridge. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.4, algebra]

- The Fox rule [F3] is the quoted literature input of [[lem-the-deficiency-one-fox-calculus-determinant-rule]]. Morton's Theorem 1 supplies the multivariable formula [F2]; steps 1.2–2.1 independently compute the equal-label Fox determinant with the library's composition order. The deletion of step 3.1 is Morton's Remark (2), with the one-variable normalization quoted in [F7].

proof_audit: The candidate G is correct in precisely the current coloured C_i(t) row basis. For both boundary rows and m=1, the same truncated ell_i calculation holds.

Every positive and negative generator is self-adjoint with respect to G in the equation C_i^TG=GC_i. This is a bilinear identity with transpose, not a Hermitian identity and not Burau's usual sesquilinear preserved form.
Transpose reverses the forward B product; repeated generator identities move G through it and produce the reverse J product. This covers mixed signs and arbitrary length.

G(1) is type-A tridiagonal Cartan matrix; its nonzero integer determinant n proves detG is not zero. It need not be a Laurent unit. Multiplicativity and integral-domain cancellation, not similarity over a fraction field, give the characteristic polynomial identity.

Local equal-label Fox determinant retains all powers of the independent axis variable x; x is not specialized until the deletion step. The (1−x^-1)/(1−x) factor cancels up to a Laurent unit, as required by the supplied Fox rule.
Multivariable characteristic determinant remains source input under exactly the labelled supplier definition, and is not deduced from the equal-label Gram identity.
Existing source-backed one-variable normalization F7 explicitly covers knots and links; no knot-only weakening is needed. Existing 3.1 and 4.1 can remain after repaired 2.1.
